---
title: "📈 Composition, stock status and trends"
description: >
  species_group_composition(), stock_status(), peak_trend(), area_overview(), regime_shift(),
  pelagic_demersal() and fao_pd_groups(): what is caught, how the stocks have developed, and when
  things changed.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("_setup.R")
FAO34 <- suppressMessages(fishing_area_data("Atlantic, Eastern Central", plot = FALSE))
```

```{r data-source, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
data_source()
```

The summary analyses take any catch data: a fishing area from `fishing_area_data()`, or any subset
of `load_fao_data()` (see [💾 FAO data](data.html)). Their charts are saved in
`figures/png/summary/` and their tables in `tables/`, with the name of the area at the start of the
file names (or `label`). Each function also returns its results invisibly, so they can be assigned
and used in R.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
FAO34 <- fishing_area_data("Atlantic, Eastern Central")
```

## ⚙️ Common arguments {#common-arguments}

Most functions of this article share these arguments; the tables of each function list only its
own arguments.

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `area_data` | FAO catch data: `fishing_area_data()$area_data`, or any subset of `load_fao_data()` (e.g. one country, or several fishing areas) | required |
| `plot` | Save the charts in `figures/png/summary/` | `TRUE` |
| `table` | Save the tables in `tables/` | `TRUE` |
| `lang` | Language of the chart text and names: `"en"`, `"zh"` or `"both"` | `NULL`: the language of `fao_settings()` (`"en"` unless changed) |
| `pptx` | Also save the charts as editable PowerPoint files in `figures/pptx/summary/` | `FALSE`; `fao_settings(pptx = TRUE)` changes it for all functions |
| `label` | Name at the start of the output file names | `NULL`: the fishing area of the data (or its country; `"selected_data"` for several areas and countries) |

## 🧺 Species group composition

`species_group_composition()` sums the catch by **ISSCAAP species group** (the FAO
classification of species into about 50 groups, such as "Herrings, sardines, anchovies") or by
**major group** (fishes, crustaceans, molluscs, ...). FAO gives no Chinese names for the groups;
the Chinese names used are unofficial translations.

```{r, figures = TRUE}
groups <- species_group_composition(FAO34$area_data)
```

The first chart shows the catch of each group, the second its share of the yearly catch. The
`top_n` largest groups are shown separately, the others combined. The table gives the mean yearly
catch of each decade, the catch of each of the last five years and the share of each group in the
last year (tonnes and %):

```{r}
show_table(groups$table, digits = 0)
```

```{r, figures = TRUE}
species_group_composition(FAO34$area_data, group = "major", lang = "zh")
```

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `group` | `"isscaap"` (ISSCAAP species groups) or `"major"` (major groups) | `"isscaap"` |
| `top_n` | Number of groups shown separately; the others are combined | `8` |
| `area_data`, `plot`, `table`, `lang`, `pptx`, `label` | See [Common arguments](#common-arguments) | |

Output: `<label>_group_isscaap.png` (or `_group_major`) and `..._share.png`, and the table
`<label>_group_isscaap.csv`; the function returns `yearly` (catch by group and year) and `table`.

## 🚦 Stock status plots

`stock_status()` classifies the catch series of each species every year, by its catch relative to
the **peak catch** of the series (Kleisner et al. 2013):

| Status | Rule |
|---|---|
| Developing | before the peak year, catch at most 50% of the peak |
| Exploited | catch above 50% of the peak |
| Over-exploited | after the peak, catch between 10% and 50% of the peak |
| Collapsed | after the peak, catch below 10% of the peak |
| Rebuilding | after a collapse, catch back between 10% and 50% of the peak |

```{r, figures = TRUE}
status <- stock_status(FAO34$area_data)
```

The first chart is the share of **stocks** in each status, the second the share of the **catch**.
A "stock" here is one species item in the data (all countries together), and years after the last
reported catch count as zero catch. Only series that meet the inclusion criteria are classified:

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `taxon_levels` | Taxonomic levels of the items included: any of `"species"`, `"genus"`, `"family"` and `"higher"` (pooled groups such as "Marine fishes nei" are `"higher"`) | `c("species", "genus", "family")` |
| `min_years` | Minimum number of years from the first to the last year with catch | `10` |
| `min_consecutive` | Minimum number of consecutive years with catch | `5` |
| `min_catch` | Minimum total catch of a series (tonnes) | `1000` |
| `smooth` | Smooth the catch with a 3-year running mean before classifying | `FALSE` |
| `area_data`, `plot`, `table`, `lang`, `pptx`, `label` | See [Common arguments](#common-arguments) | |

The table of stocks gives the peak year and the status of each stock in the last year:

```{r}
show_table(status$stocks, digits = 0)
table(status$stocks$status_last_year)
```

```{r, figures = TRUE}
# Smoothed catches, stricter inclusion
stock_status(FAO34$area_data, smooth = TRUE, min_catch = 10000, label = "FAO34 smoothed")
```

Output: `<label>_stock_status_stocks.png` and `<label>_stock_status_catch.png`, and the tables
`<label>_stock_status.csv` (stocks and catch by status and year) and
`<label>_stock_status_stocks.csv`; the function returns `yearly`, `stocks` and `status` (the
status of each stock in each year).

::: callout-note
Stock status plots use catch data only. A falling catch can also come from management,
markets or reporting, so the results are indicative and do not replace stock assessments.
:::

## ⛰️ Peak and trend

`peak_trend()` finds, for the total and for the main species (or countries, or areas), the year and
size of the **peak catch**, the catch in the last year as a **percentage of the peak**, and the
trend over the last `recent_years` years:

- **growth rate** (`growth_pct_per_year`): the average yearly growth between the first and the
  last of these years, $100\,[(C_n/C_1)^{1/(n-1)} - 1]$, with $C_1$ and $C_n$ the catch of the
  first and the last of the $n$ years;
- **trend**: a Mann-Kendall test (Mann 1945; Kendall 1975), Kendall's τ between year and catch;
  `trend` is `"up"` or `"down"` when p < 0.05, otherwise `"none"`.

```{r, figures = TRUE}
species_trend <- peak_trend(FAO34$area_data, by = "species", top_n = 10)
```

```{r}
show_table(species_trend[, c("name", "peak_year", "pct_of_peak", "growth_pct_per_year", "kendall_tau", "p_value", "trend")])
```

```{r, figures = TRUE}
peak_trend(FAO34$area_data, by = "country", top_n = 15, recent_years = 20, lang = "zh")
```

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `by` | What to compare: `"species"`, `"country"` or `"area"` | `"species"` |
| `top_n` | Number of series with the largest total catch (`Inf` for all) | `10` |
| `recent_years` | Number of most recent years used for the trend | `10` |
| `area_data`, `plot`, `table`, `lang`, `pptx`, `label` | See [Common arguments](#common-arguments) | |

Output: `<label>_peak_trend_species.png` (or `_country`, `_area`) and the table with the same
name; the function returns a data frame with one row per series, the total first.

## 🌍 All FAO marine areas

`area_overview()` compares all FAO marine fishing areas: the catch of each area over time with its
peak, and the peak and trend chart of `peak_trend(by = "area")` for the areas:

```{r, figures = TRUE}
overview <- area_overview()
```

```{r}
show_table(overview[, c("name", "peak_year", "peak_tonnes", "last_year_tonnes", "pct_of_peak", "trend")], n = 20, digits = 0)
```

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `recent_years` | Number of most recent years used for the trend | `10` |
| `data_version` | FAO data release to use (see `load_fao_data()`) | `"latest"` |
| `plot`, `table`, `lang`, `pptx` | See [Common arguments](#common-arguments) | |

`area_overview()` reads the FAO data itself, so it has no `area_data` or `label`. Output:
`marine_areas_catch.png`, `marine_areas_peak_trend_area.png` and the table
`marine_areas_peak_trend_area.csv`; the function returns the data frame of `peak_trend()`.

## 🔀 Synchronous breakpoints

`regime_shift()` runs a breakpoint analysis on the catch series of the main species (all species
items, including "nei" groups) and counts how many species change their mean catch in each year.
Each series is split where its mean changes (`strucchange::breakpoints()`, Bai and Perron 2003;
Zeileis et al. 2002, 2003), with the number of breakpoints chosen by BIC; the year of a
breakpoint is the first year of the new period. Years when many species change together may point
to an ecosystem-wide regime shift, or to changes in management or reporting.

```{r, figures = TRUE}
shifts <- regime_shift(FAO34$area_data, top_n = 20)
```

```{r}
show_table(shifts$breakpoints[, c("species", "first_year", "n_breakpoints", "breakpoint_years")], n = 20)
head(shifts$yearly[order(-shifts$yearly$n_species), ], 5)
```

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `top_n` | Number of species with the largest total catch that are analysed | `20` |
| `h_value` | Minimum length of a period between breakpoints: a fraction of the series length or a number of years | `0.15` |
| `area_data`, `plot`, `table`, `lang`, `pptx`, `label` | See [Common arguments](#common-arguments) | |

Species whose series is too short for `h_value` are skipped with a message. Output:
`<label>_regime_shift.png` (number of species with a breakpoint in each year),
`<label>_regime_shift_species.png` (breakpoints of each species), and the tables
`<label>_regime_shift.csv` and `<label>_regime_shift_years.csv`; the function returns
`breakpoints` and `yearly`.

## 🐟 Pelagic/demersal ratio

`pelagic_demersal()` divides the catch of pelagic fishes by the catch of demersal fishes (P/D) in
each FAO marine area, by year and by decade. Caddy (1993) proposed that nutrient enrichment
favours short-lived plankton-feeding pelagic fishes over demersal fishes, and de Leiva Moreno
et al. (2000) used P/D as a proxy for the nutrient level of the seas around Europe. The ratio of a
decade is the mean of its yearly ratios (as Hondorp et al. 2010), with the lowest and the highest.

```{r, figures = "pelagic_demersal_ratio"}
pd <- pelagic_demersal(FAO34$area_data)
```

```{r}
show_table(pd$decades[, c("period", "pd_mean", "pd_min", "pd_max", "counted_pct")])
show_table(pd$groups[, c("group", "counted_as", "catch_pct")], n = 12)
```

The FAO data give each species an ISSCAAP species group, so the function counts groups.
`fao_pd_groups()` shows how each group is counted by the two published definitions (it has no
arguments):

| `definition` | Pelagic | Demersal |
|---|---|---|
| `"de_leiva_moreno"` (default) | Herrings, sardines, anchovies (small pelagics) | Flounders, cods and hakes, miscellaneous coastal and demersal fishes, marine crustaceans except krill |
| `"grainger_garcia"` (Grainger and Garcia 1996) | Small pelagics, tunas and billfishes, miscellaneous pelagic fishes | Flounders, cods and hakes, miscellaneous coastal and demersal fishes, sharks and rays, unidentified marine fishes |

```{r}
show_table(fao_pd_groups(), n = 15)
```

Your own groups can be given with `pelagic = ...` and `demersal = ...`. The published studies
classed each species rather than ISSCAAP groups, so their values (below 1 in oligotrophic seas,
about 1 to 3.5 in mesotrophic and about 6 to 20 in eutrophic seas, in de Leiva Moreno et al.
2000) are only roughly comparable. P/D also changes with fishing and markets (demersal fishes
are in higher demand; Caddy et al. 1998), hypoxia (Hondorp et al. 2010), the natural variability
of small pelagics and reporting; see `?pelagic_demersal`. In area 34, the large catch of small
pelagics in upwelling waters keeps P/D high.

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `definition` | Groups counted as pelagic and demersal: `"de_leiva_moreno"` or `"grainger_garcia"` | `"de_leiva_moreno"` |
| `pelagic`, `demersal` | Your own ISSCAAP groups (English names as in the FAO data, e.g. `"Herrings, sardines, anchovies"`) instead of those of `definition` | `NULL` |
| `by` | `"area"`, or `"division"` for the catch by division of `load_fao_divisions()` (🧩 extension) | `"area"` |
| `area_data`, `plot`, `table`, `lang`, `pptx`, `label` | See [Common arguments](#common-arguments) | |

Inland areas are left out with a message. Output: `<label>_pelagic_demersal_ratio.png` (P/D by
year, one panel per area), `<label>_pelagic_demersal.png` and `..._share.png` (pelagic,
demersal and other catch), and the tables `<label>_pelagic_demersal.csv`, `..._decades.csv` and
`..._groups.csv`; the function returns `yearly`, `decades` and `groups`.

### 🧩 By division (extension)

De Leiva Moreno et al. (2000) compared the divisions of the Mediterranean and Black Sea. The same
units are available from the catch data of regional fishery bodies, loaded with
`load_fao_divisions()` (an extension of the package, not part of the Word report; see
[🚢 Trade and employment](trade-employment.html) for the other datasets):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
pelagic_demersal(load_fao_divisions("GFCM"), by = "division")
```

In release 2026.1.0, the mean P/D of the 1980s is below 1 in the Ionian (0.6) and the Levant
(0.4), about 4 in the Adriatic and about 18 in the Black Sea, within the ranges de Leiva Moreno
et al. (2000) found for oligotrophic, mesotrophic and eutrophic seas.

## 📝 In the Word report

`fao_report()` writes these analyses into the Word report of a fishing area (see
[📝 Assessment report: Word, LaTeX and PDF](report.html)). The ISSCAAP groups (`groups = TRUE`) and the stock
status plots (`status = TRUE`) are sections by default; the pelagic/demersal ratio is added with
`pelagic = TRUE`. The settings of a function are given with the section name as prefix, e.g.
`status_smooth = TRUE` is `smooth = TRUE` of `stock_status()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fao_report(34, pelagic = TRUE, status_smooth = TRUE, pelagic_definition = "grainger_garcia")
```

`peak_trend()` gives the trends in the tables of the main species and countries of the report;
`area_overview()` and `regime_shift()` are not part of it.
